title: MCP Server
markdown:
Open Executive can run **as an MCP server**, the inverse of the MCP *gateway* (which lets the Executive consume external MCP servers). The server exposes Open Executive's company-grounded context and its specialist council to external MCP clients — Claude Desktop, Cursor, Claude Code, or any other agent — so they can ground themselves in *this* company and pull domain analysis **inside their own loop**, without re-explaining anything.

This is deliberately *not* another chat channel: Open Executive already has six of those (web, Slack, Discord, Telegram, email, Google Chat). The value here is structured, attachable context plus on-demand specialist analysis.

## Transport & mount

The server speaks **Streamable-HTTP** and is mounted into the existing FastAPI app at `/mcp` (built with the `FastMCP` SDK, `streamable_http_path="/"` mounted under `/mcp` so the endpoint is exactly `/mcp`). Mounting a sub-app does not run its lifespan, so the API lifespan runs `mcp.session_manager.run()` for the life of the process — without it every `/mcp` request would fail. The module lives at `openexecutive/mcp_server/` and is wired in `api/main.py`.

## Auth

The `/mcp` endpoint is **not** exempt from the shared-secret middleware, so it is gated exactly like every other route: clients send `x-api-key: $BACKEND_SHARED_SECRET`. There is no second auth system. FastMCP's DNS-rebinding (Host-header) check is disabled because the endpoint authenticates with a header secret rather than a cookie — a browser rebinding attack cannot supply the key — and traffic arrives through the deployment's TLS terminator.

## Resources (read-only context)

The highest-value surface: curated company state, pure reads, no LLM calls.

| Resource URI | Contents |
|---|---|
| `oe://company/profile` | Structured company profile, as a prompt block |
| `oe://today/briefing` | Morning-brief snapshot: department health, roster, proposals |
| `oe://today/activity` | Recent self-initiated Executive activity |
| `oe://people/roster` | Active people on the roster |
| `oe://departments/state` | Departments with goals and cadences |
| `oe://memory/decisions` · `…/initiatives` · `…/advice` | Episodic memory |
| `oe://talent/engagements` | Active executive-search engagements, rolled up by pipeline stage |

## Tools (capabilities)

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `consult_specialist(specialist, query, context)` | **Flagship.** Domain analysis from one of ten specialists (cso, cfo, chro, gc, coo, cmo, cpo, board_comms, talent, triage), each grounded in company knowledge. Stateless. |
| `search_knowledge(query)` | Raw retrieval over the MBA knowledge base + indexed company docs |
| `list_workflows()` | Catalog of multi-step executive workflows and their input schemas |
| `ask_executive(message, caller_email?)` | A single synthesized Executive answer — a fallback; prefer the specialist tool and resources |
| `list_candidates(engagement_id, stage?)` · `get_candidate(candidate_id)` | Browse one executive-search engagement's candidate pipeline (read-only) |
| `match_candidates(engagement_id, limit?)` · `find_similar_candidates(candidate_id, limit?)` | Semantic candidate search over the talent graph — ranked, name-enriched results |

The talent suite is **read-only**: it reads `talent.store` and ranks via `talent.graph`, the same data layer the `/talent` UI and the briefing use. Candidate writes and workflow runs are not exposed (see below). The `talent` specialist's *advice* is reachable via `consult_specialist`.

## What's intentionally deferred

**Workflow *execution*** is not exposed over MCP yet. Workflows are long-running async generators (minutes), which would exceed a single tool call's request/response window. The catalog is listed via `list_workflows()`; if execution is added later it will use a job-handle pattern (`start_workflow` → `run_id`, then poll) over the existing run persistence. MCP *prompts* are also skipped — OE workflows are server-executed orchestrations, not message templates.

## Why prompt caching is unaffected

This path is parallel to chat. Resources are pure reads; `consult_specialist` delegates to the same `BaseAgent.analyze` that the chat path uses, reusing the existing cached system blocks. Nothing here touches the cache layout.

The `specialist` argument is **resolved, not merely matched**, using the same `router.resolve_specialist_name` the chat path uses — so a re-cased or truncated name (`csO`, `cs`) reaches the intended specialist here exactly as it does in chat. An exact-membership check would have given external clients a stricter, divergent policy and would also have skipped the `routing_anomaly` audit row.

That tolerance has to be spelled in the **type hint**, not just in the handler. FastMCP builds a Pydantic model from the tool signature and validates arguments against it before the handler body runs, so while `specialist` was annotated as a bare `Literal` of the ten registry keys, `csO` was refused at the schema layer with a `literal_error` and the resolver never ran — the parity above was documented but not delivered. The parameter is therefore typed `str` with the roster attached as `json_schema_extra={"enum": ...}`: clients still see the exact ten values in the advertised tool schema, *server-side* validation no longer rejects anything outside them, and the **raw** name is forwarded to `route_to_specialist`, which is where the correction and its `routing_anomaly` row are recorded. The tolerance is server-side only by design — the advertised schema still carries `enum`, so a client that validates outbound arguments against it will still refuse to send `csO` before the request leaves, which is the right behaviour for a client that can tell the name is wrong. What the widening buys is the case the resolver was written for: a *model* emitting a truncated name through a client that passes arguments straight through. Normalising at the validator boundary would have kept the enum too, but it would have erased the anomaly it exists to log. A name that genuinely resolves to nothing still raises `ValueError` rather than returning prose: an MCP caller is a program that wants an error, not a model that wants a recoverable `tool_result`.
